newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Trouble-free night in Albania after election.
newsitem.headline: Trouble-free night in Albania after election.

text.p: Albania remained calm on Monday following a bitterly-contested general election in which Socialists claim to have won a resounding victory, but no official results have so far been announced.
Tirana citizens heeded warnings by the Interior Ministry not to stage celebrations in the capital and few people were on the streets after dark on Sunday night.

There were more sounds of gunfire in Tirana than the usual nightly shooting in the air but by morning there were no reports of any injuries. Armoured police vehicles patrolled the streets through the night.
The calm contrasted sharply with noisy celebrations in the Adriatic port of Sarande where Socialists appeared to have won more than 50 percent of the vote.
Sarande central square was littered with spent cartridges after hours of shooting that lasted until 5 a.m. A local election official told reporters not to be concerned.
"This is not a war but jubilation," he said.

President Sali Berisha's Democrats, who dominated the last parliament after last year's disputed general election, appeared downcast but said it was far too early for the Socialists to say they have triumphed.
"We are doing less well than we thought but we are still waiting for the results," Democrat secretary-general Genc Pollo told reporters.

Socialist leader Fatos Nano, released from jail in March three years after what was widely considered a suspect trial, said on Sunday night his party's data showed it had won 60 of 115 seats contested under majority voting in Sunday's election.

With expectations of gaining at least half the remaining 40 seats shared out under a proportional system, Nano said the Socialists and allied leftist parties would hold a two-thirds majority in parliament.
"A centre-left coalition will control two-thirds of the new parliament for sure," Nano told reporters amid jubilation at his party's headquarters in central Tirana.
The central electoral commission said turnout appeared to be more than 60 percent.

Albanians were also asked to vote in a referendum on whether to replace the republic with a constitutional monarchy. The monarchist party on Monday claimed they had clinched a majority of votes around the country, enabling Leka, son of Zog, Albania's king from 1928 to 1939, to assume the throne.
But, as with the general election results, it was too early to forecast the outcome one way or the other.
Berisha confirmed on Sunday he would respect the election results but he and Nano have made clear they would not be able to work together.
Whatever the outcome, any new government has an uphill task to restore order in swathes of southern Albania which remain in the grip of gangs, criminal cliques and local mafia warlords.

Officials of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) and the Council of Europe, who assisted Albanian authorities in organising the election, appeared happy with the way polling had been conducted.

Senior OSCE representative Catherine Lalumiere and OSCE and Council of Europe officials toured Albania on Sunday to hear accounts of the voting from some of the 500 international observers and Albanian electoral officials.

Observers were escorted by some of the 7,000 soldiers of a multinational protection force deployed in Albania in April after weeks of violence, looting and killings sparked by the collapse of pyramid investment schemes. Some 1,500 people have been killed in the violence in the Balkan state.
"The procedures, from what we have seen and heard, were satisfactory and the turnout very good, up to 80 percent in some areas," said Lalumiere.

Problems were also reported with electoral registers and delivery of ballot papers in outlying areas, but the election had none of the voter intimidation and ballot stuffing which marred last year's election.
Lalumiere was due to give an early idea of observers' findings at a news conference at 3 p.m. (1300 GMT) on Monday.
